chunks.title: Approach to microbial keratitis
chunks.tldr: History is half the diagnosis: trauma, contact lens wear, topical steroids (open the door to bacteria, fungi, HSV), past HSV. Slitlamp + fluorescein. Scrape before treating: Gram & Giemsa, cultures (bacteria, fungi, Acanthamoeba on non-nutrient agar + E coli), PCR for HSV/Acanthamoeba/fungi. Start treatment as soon as samples are taken; read lab results alongside the clinical picture.
points: Imaging: topography (shape), specular microscopy (endothelial count), AS-OCT (depth, graft position), confocal microscopy (Acanthamoeba cysts, fungal hyphae).
Recurrent erosion hurts; recurrent HSV often doesn't (reduced sensation).

cards.q: Which imaging tool can directly show Acanthamoeba cysts and fungal hyphae?
cards.a: In vivo confocal microscopy.

chunks.title: Bacterial ulcers by bug
chunks.tldr: Pneumococcus: 24–48 h after abrasion, creeping ulcer toward centre, clear surrounding cornea, hypopyon; lancet-shaped G+ diplococci; look for dacryocystitis. Pseudomonas: soft CL / overnight wear, rapid melt from proteolytic enzymes, big hypopyon, perforation risk; G– rods. Moraxella: indolent inferior oval ulcer in alcoholics/diabetics; square-ended G– diplobacilli. Staph/α-strep: indolent, in steroid-compromised corneas; infectious crystalline keratopathy (branching) with long-term steroids. Nocardia / M chelonae: soil trauma, 'cracked windshield' ulcer bed.
points: Rx (Table 6-3): topical fluoroquinolone hourly day & night 48 h → hourly by day ×3 d → qds; 2nd line fortified cefuroxime 5% + gentamicin 1.5%.
Mycobacterial: amikacin 2.5% + levofloxacin; chlamydial: oral azithro/doxy.

cards.q: Infectious crystalline keratopathy is associated with which organism and which drug?
cards.a: Alpha-haemolytic (viridans) streptococci, in corneas on long-term topical steroid (often grafts).

cards.q: Second-line fortified antibiotics for bacterial keratitis per Vaughan?
cards.a: Cefuroxime 5% and gentamicin 1.5%.

chunks.title: Fungal & Acanthamoeba keratitis
chunks.tldr: Fungal: vegetable-matter trauma, CL, steroids. Feathery irregular edge, raised dry infiltrate, satellite lesions, endothelial plaque, hypopyon. Filamentous (Fusarium, Aspergillus) → natamycin 5%; yeasts (Candida) → amphotericin 0.15%; second line voriconazole 1%. Steroids contraindicated. Acanthamoeba: CL + tap water/swimming; pain out of proportion, perineural infiltrates early, ring infiltrate later; often misdiagnosed as HSV. Rx: PHMB 0.02% and/or hexamidine/propamidine (must be cysticidal), hourly then tapered over months.
points: Corneal biopsy beats scraping for Acanthamoeba; culture the lens case.
Keratoplasty if progressing; scleral spread does badly.
chunks.hook: Agony + small epithelial changes + lens wearer = Acanthamoeba.

cards.q: First-line topical drug for filamentous fungal keratitis?
cards.a: Natamycin 5%.

cards.q: Early sign of Acanthamoeba keratitis on slitlamp?
cards.a: Radial perineural infiltrates (keratoneuritis).

chunks.title: HSV keratitis: forms
chunks.tldr: HSV-1 latent in trigeminal ganglion; triggers: fever, UV, trauma, menses, stress. Epithelial: dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs → broader geographic ulcer (esp. after steroids); reduced corneal sensation. Stromal: necrotising (viral replication, can perforate) vs disciform (commonest; central disc of oedema, KPs underneath, immune). Endotheliitis: oedema + KPs + raised IOP + iritis. Peripheral HSV ulcer: epithelium lost before infiltrate (opposite of staph marginal).
points: Bilateral in 4–6%, mostly atopic patients.
Primary HSV in kids: vesicular blepharoconjunctivitis.
chunks.hook: Dendrite has bulbs on its tips; zoster pseudodendrite doesn't.

cards.q: Most common form of HSV stromal keratitis?
cards.a: Disciform keratitis (immune-mediated central disc of stromal oedema).

cards.q: How do you distinguish peripheral HSV ulcer from staph marginal keratitis?
cards.a: HSV: epithelial loss precedes infiltrate, little pain/photophobia; staph: infiltrate first with clear zone, painful.

chunks.title: HSV keratitis: treatment
chunks.tldr: Epithelial: debride infected epithelium + topical ganciclovir/acyclovir/trifluridine, or oral acyclovir. Oral acyclovir doses: 400 mg 5×/day active (800 mg 5×/day if immunocompromised/atopic); prophylaxis 400 mg bd. Stromal/disciform: topical steroid only under antiviral cover, ophthalmologist-supervised. Graft only after months of quiescence, with oral antiviral cover; DALK preferred (less rejection).
points: Over-treatment with many drops → epithelial toxicity; often improves by simplifying.
Small perforation: cyanoacrylate glue; persistent defect: BCL, tarsorrhaphy, amniotic membrane.
chunks.hook: Steroid for HSV stroma? Never without an antiviral umbrella.

cards.q: Prophylactic oral acyclovir dose for recurrent HSV keratitis?
cards.a: 400 mg twice daily.

chunks.title: Zoster & adenoviral keratitis
chunks.tldr: HZO: Hutchinson sign (nasociliary tip-of-nose rash) predicts eye involvement. Stroma and uvea hit from the start; blotchy epithelium, pseudodendrites, nummular/disciform keratitis, uveitis, sclerokeratitis, neurotrophic cornea for months. Rx within 72 h: acyclovir 800 mg 5×/d ×10–14 d / valacyclovir 1 g tds / famciclovir 500 mg tds ×7–10 d; topical steroid for keratitis/uveitis. Adenovirus: punctate keratitis day 5–7, then SEIs at day 8–15 lasting months; steroids clear but rebound; cyclosporine/tacrolimus alternative.
points: Elderly get severe zoster disease; children mild.
Follow zoster patients for months — keratitis may appear late.
chunks.hook: Tip of the nose blisters = check the eye.

cards.q: Why is the cornea at risk long after zoster keratitis seems healed?
cards.a: Loss of corneal sensation → neurotrophic keratitis/ulceration and secondary infection.

chunks.title: Marginal keratitis, Mooren & PUK
chunks.tldr: Marginal (catarrhal) keratitis: immune reaction to staph antigens; oval infiltrate with clear zone from limbus, painful, 7–10 d; Rx lid hygiene ± weak steroid. Mooren ulcer: idiopathic autoimmune, painful circumferential undermined excavation, elderly, unilateral 60–80%; needs systemic immunosuppression, conjunctival resection, tectonic graft. PUK: peripheral melt with systemic vasculitis — RA, GPA (Wegener), PAN, SLE, relapsing polychondritis, IBD; immune complexes in limbal capillaries (like glomeruli). Treat the systemic disease.
points: Rule out HSV before steroid for a marginal infiltrate.
Perforation: glue, patch graft, keratoplasty.
chunks.hook: Peripheral melt = look for vasculitis; it may be life-threatening.

cards.q: Systemic diseases associated with peripheral ulcerative keratitis?
cards.a: Rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, polyarteritis nodosa, SLE, relapsing polychondritis, IBD.

chunks.title: Vitamin A, neurotrophic, exposure & toxic keratopathy
chunks.tldr: Xerophthalmia: night blindness, Bitot spots (foamy temporal keratinised wedge), bilateral central grey ulcer → keratomalacia and perforation; malnutrition/malabsorption; Rx vitamin A (adult mild 30,000 U/d ×1 wk). Neurotrophic (CN V damage): painless epithelial breakdown → ulcer; Rx lubricate, close the lids (taping, tarsorrhaphy, botox ptosis), nerve growth factor drops, serum. Exposure: inferior third ulcer (proptosis, Bell palsy, ectropion). Toxic: trifluridine, aminoglycosides, BAK → inferior coarse punctate keratitis.
points: Anaesthesia + exposure together = worst combination.
Dry eye: filaments in the lower cornea.
chunks.hook: Numb cornea can't complain — warn the patient to report redness.

cards.q: What is a Bitot spot?
cards.a: A foamy, triangular area of keratinised temporal bulbar conjunctiva in vitamin A deficiency.

cards.q: Topical biologic for neurotrophic keratitis?
cards.a: Nerve growth factor (cenegermin) drops.

chunks.title: Keratoconus
chunks.tldr: Bilateral asymmetric stromal thinning/protrusion; starts teens. Associations: Down, atopy/eye rubbing, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, RP. Rising myopic irregular astigmatism, scissoring reflex. Signs: Vogt striae (pathognomonic), Fleischer ring (iron), Munson sign; topography detects early (forme fruste — no LASIK!). Acute hydrops = Descemet break, clears with scar. Rx: glasses → rigid CL; corneal cross-linking (riboflavin + UVA) halts progression; ring segments; DALK/PK when CL fails.
points: Review every 6–12 months with serial topography to catch progression.
Graft outcomes good: >85% good vision at 4 years.
chunks.hook: Progressing cone? Cross-link it before it needs a graft.

cards.q: Pathognomonic slitlamp sign of keratoconus?
cards.a: Vogt striae — fine vertical folds in deep stroma/Descemet that disappear with pressure.

cards.q: What does corneal collagen cross-linking use?
cards.a: Riboflavin drops plus ultraviolet A light to strengthen stromal collagen bonds.

chunks.title: Corneal degenerations
chunks.tldr: Terrien: men, superior marginal thinning with vessels + lipid leading edge, painless, slow. Band keratopathy: calcium in Bowman's, interpalpebral with clear rim and holes; JIA uveitis, chronic inflammation, hypercalcaemia/hyperparathyroidism; Rx scrape + EDTA chelation ± PTK. Spheroidal (climatic droplet): UV, outdoor workers, golden droplets. Salzmann nodules: grey-white elevated nodules after phlyctenules/trachoma. Arcus: grey ring with clear zone; check lipids if <50.
points: Vortex keratopathy (verticillata): amiodarone, chloroquine/HCQ, indomethacin, phenothiazines, Fabry.
chunks.hook: Band keratopathy in a child = JIA until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Treatment of calcific band keratopathy?
cards.a: Epithelial removal and chelation with EDTA (0.01 M), ± excimer PTK smoothing.

cards.q: Drugs causing cornea verticillata?
cards.a: Amiodarone, chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, indomethacin, phenothiazines (also Fabry disease).

chunks.title: Corneal dystrophies (IC3D)
chunks.tldr: Bilateral, symmetric, inherited, no inflammation. Epithelial: EBMD (map-dot-fingerprint; recurrent erosions), Meesmann (keratin K3/K12). Epithelial-stromal TGFBI (5q31, AD): Reis-Bücklers (Bowman's, erosions), lattice (branching lines, amyloid, erosions, recurs in graft), granular (breadcrumbs, hyaline, clear between). Stromal: macular (AR, CHST6, mucopolysaccharide, hazy to limbus, worst vision), Schnyder (UBIAD1, crystals). Endothelial: Fuchs, PPCD (AD; vesicles, ZEB1), CHED (AR, SLC4A11).
points: Lattice and EBMD/Reis-Bücklers cause recurrent erosions.
Transplant usually restores vision; lattice/granular can recur in the graft.
chunks.hook: Marilyn Monroe Always Gets Her Man in LA City: Macular–Mucopolysaccharide–Alcian; Granular–Hyaline; Lattice–Amyloid–Congo.

cards.q: The only autosomal recessive classic stromal dystrophy?
cards.a: Macular corneal dystrophy (CHST6).

cards.q: Which gene underlies Reis-Bücklers, Thiel-Behnke, lattice type 1 and granular dystrophies?
cards.a: TGFBI on 5q31.

chunks.title: Fuchs, Thygeson & recurrent erosion
chunks.tldr: Fuchs: women, 4th decade+; central guttae, thick Descemet, endothelial loss → morning blur/glare that clears through the day → stromal/epithelial oedema, bullae; decompensates after cataract surgery. Rx: hypertonic saline, then endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK/DMEK) ± combined with cataract. Thygeson SPK: bilateral raised grey oval central epithelial dots, white quiet eye, recurrent for years; weak steroid or cyclosporine. Recurrent erosion: wakes with pain on eye opening; trauma, EBMD; Rx lubricant ointment for months, 5% NaCl, BCL, anterior stromal puncture, PTK.
points: Erosion = faulty hemidesmosome anchoring of epithelium to Bowman's.
Staph keratitis: lower third; trachoma: upper third; Thygeson: central, no conjunctivitis.
chunks.hook: Fuchs = foggy at Five a.m., clearer by noon.

cards.q: Why is vision worse in the morning in Fuchs dystrophy?
cards.a: Overnight corneal oedema with lids closed (no evaporation); clears as tears evaporate during the day.

cards.q: Surgical options for recurrent corneal erosion resistant to lubricants?
cards.a: Bandage CL, anterior stromal puncture, excimer phototherapeutic keratectomy.

chunks.title: Limbal stem cell deficiency & keratoplasty types
chunks.tldr: LSCD: chemical/thermal burns, SJS, pemphigoid, GVHD, aniridia, CL overuse, drop toxicity → conjunctivalisation, vessels, persistent defects. Impression cytology: goblet cells + CK19 = conjunctival; CK3/12 = corneal. Rx: limbal transplant (autologous from fellow eye — CLAU/SLET, or allogeneic), cultivated cells, amniotic membrane. Grafts: PK (full thickness), DALK (keep own Descemet/endothelium — keratoconus, stromal scars, no endothelial rejection), DSAEK/DMEK (endothelial failure), tectonic, rotational.
points: Donor cornea storage: 4°C up to ~10 days; organ culture 34°C up to ~6 weeks.
Biggest PK problems: astigmatism and rejection.

cards.q: Which keratoplasty is preferred for Fuchs dystrophy?
cards.a: Endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK or DMEK).

cards.q: Impression cytology markers of conjunctivalised cornea?
cards.a: Goblet cells and cytokeratin 19 (instead of corneal CK3/CK12).

chunks.title: Refractive corneal surgery
chunks.tldr: LASIK: flap (femtosecond/microkeratome) + excimer ablation of bed — fastest recovery; risk of ectasia with large ablations/thin corneas; flap complications. PRK/surface ablation: epithelium removed then ablated — for thin corneas and contact sports; more pain, haze risk. Wavefront-guided refines. Intrastromal ring segments (Intacs/KeraRing) for keratoconus CL intolerance; arcuate keratotomy for astigmatism (incl. post-graft).
points: Prior refractive surgery makes IOL power calculation tricky.
Forme fruste keratoconus on topography = no LASIK.
chunks.hook: Thin cornea or boxer? PRK, not LASIK.

cards.q: Key screening finding that contraindicates LASIK?
cards.a: Forme fruste keratoconus / abnormal topography or thin cornea (ectasia risk).
